newsitem.title: UK: Reuters buyback to curb cash growth.
newsitem.headline: Reuters buyback to curb cash growth.

text.p: Global news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc on Wednesday announced plans to repurchase shares worth up to 200 million pounds ($335.8 million) over the next 12 months.

Reuters said the strong pound caused a three percent dip in profit in the first six months of 1997 for the company, which generates more than 80 percent of its income overseas. Pre-tax profit fell to 333 million pounds from 342 million a year earlier but was 12 percent higher if measured at comparable exchange rates.

Chief executive Peter Job said the buy-back sum, which will offset growth in the company's 1.12 billion pounds cash mountain, was the maximum it could return to shareholders efficiently under British tax rules.
"If you go beyond a certain limit you simply get involved in unrecoverable tax, which is not very good for shareholders," Job said in an interview.
Job said underlying revenue growth in the six months was in line with 1996 at eight percent and was expected to remain around this level for 1997 as a whole.
The company said it did not expect the pound to hit its market positioning, but currency factors were likely to continue to restrict reported revenue and earnings.
Reuters increased its interim dividend by 13 percent to 3.1 pence and said it expected to maintain double digit dividend growth in 1997.
The profit figure was towards the bottom end of analysts' forecasts and Reuters shares fell 16p to 593.5p by early afternoon, giving up gains ahead of the figures.
Analysts and dealers said the results had not provided enough positive surprises to allow the stock to build on its recent rally. It has lately rebounded from a year low of 555p set on July 10.
"The numbers are all right but the fact that they (profits) are down and they are only distributing 200 million has disappointed the market," said NatWest analyst Neill Junor.
Reuters was forced last October to scrap plans to return 613 million pounds to shareholders after the then government changed tax rules.
Job said Reuters would continue to seek a way through what he termed a "maze of tax and other regulations" in order to return more of its cash surplus to shareholders.
The company said it believed the British system should be brought in line with that in the U.S. to allow companies to acquire their own shares in a tax neutral manner without having to cancel them.

Reuters forecast a slight decline in margins over the next two years as it gears up for European monetary union and the new millennium. Job said the millennium would be an opportunity to phase out obsolete products and identified the Internet as a potential growth area.

Revenue fell by 29 million pounds to 1.41 billion in the half but rose by eight percent at comparable exchange rates. Underlying margins were maintained despite the cost of rolling out the new 3000 range of products.
Installations of the 3000 series, slow to begin with, picked up strongly. Orders now total 24,300, of which 10,600 have been installed.
Information products grew revenue by seven percent year on year at comparable exchange rates and improved market share.
Transaction products revenue grew by 10 percent at comparable rates, with revenue at Instinet, the electronic equity brokerage, ahead by 17 percent.
Revenue from the Dealing 2000 foreign exchange products rose by four percent at comparable rates. ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
